Required modelling capabilities for newly diversified field arrangements in heterogeneous fields and landscapes * 4.1 Crop species/cultivars options in agroecosystem models * 4.2 Field classification into smaller units considering soil heterogeneities for site-specific management * 4.3 Impact of diversified field arrangements on biotic stressors * 4.4 Agriculture 4.0 * 4.5 Ecosystem services and biodiversity * 5. Concluding remarks * Declarations * References * 6. Tables and figures 1 Introduction Agriculture in Germany is highly productive and characterized by increasingly mechanized large farms (average farm size in 2020 was 64 ha), producing 50 billion Euros in goods per year (Destatis 2021). Crop rotations have been simplified in the last decades (Barbieri et al. 2017) due to the introduction of mineral fertilizers, plant protection products (PPPs), and progress in plant breeding, which allows farmers to rely less on crop rotations for pest and weed control (Andert et al. 2016; Melander et al. 2013). Crop production patterns have been additionally influenced by farm specialization, market demands, priority for short-term profitability, availability of labor (Gutzler et al. 2015), and agricultural policies (Bauböck et al. 2014; Steinmann and Dobers 2013). The resulting systems are heavily dependent on external inputs and have led to a series of environmental problems jeopardizing the ecosystem service (ESS) delivery, related to provisioning of food, fiber, fuel, soil fertility, and water quality (Barbieri et al. 2017; Stoate et al. 2001). Excessive PPP application has caused detrimental effects to biodiversity and pollution of water bodies (Concepcion et al. 2020; Dudley et al. 2017; Tang et al. 2021). Moreover, the yield losses and yield variability associated with climatic extremes increased in recent years (Luttger and Feike 2018; Olesen et al. 2011; Webber et al. 2020). Spatial and temporal crop diversification of cropping systems offer multiple benefits to the delivery of ESS, with mostly positive impacts on soil fertility and structure (Tamburini et al. 2020), crop yield (Anderson 2005), yield stability (Gaudin et al. 2015; Weih et al. 2021; Zampieri et al. 2020), nitrogen (N) cycling (Luce et al. 2020), carbon sequestration (Hazra et al. 2019; Tamburini et al. 2020), pest control (Letourneau et al. 2011; Lin 2011), biodiversity (Beillouin et al. 2021), and reduced yield risk (Feliciano 2019; Gaudin et al. 2015). Realizing greater benefit from crop diversification in these regards can be supported with the development of field robotics in the coming years allowing smaller field sizes and diversified agricultural landscapes. The resulting multifunctional landscapes would balance benefits and tradeoffs in ESS through consideration of natural variabilities in soils and other site characteristics (Basso and Antle 2020). Smaller field sizes (i.e., patches) are associated with multiple benefits to ecosystems, especially for biodiversity and species richness (Concepcion et al. 2020; Fahrig et al. 2015; Torres et al. 2020). Diversified landscapes via smaller patches (field units with a particular structure and function within the landscape), and additional landscape elements (i.e., hedgerows, flower strips) promote farmland biodiversity and pest regulation (Albrecht et al. 2020; Fahrig et al. 2015; Salek et al. 2018; Scheiner and Martin 2020; Sirami et al. 2019; Tscharntke et al. 2021). Spatial and temporal diversification in new field arrangements considering soil heterogeneity across landscapes can be an option to improve resource use efficiency as resources can be allocated according to the specific field characteristics in turn improving the delivery of ESS (Basso et al. 2013; Kersebaum et al. 2005; Tripathi et al. 2015). Agroecosystem models are mathematical tools that simulate crop growth and development and soil processes in response to environmental conditions (radiation, temperature, water availability and retention, atmospheric CO2, and nutrient availability from soils) and management practices (crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, etc.), typically using daily time step routines (Muller and Martre 2019; Rotter et al. 2015). They started to be developed in the 1960s and have evolved to include more complex approaches with improved representation of soil-plant-atmosphere dynamics. Agroecosystem modelling can be a powerful complementary method to field experiments, as virtual experiments can inform subsequent field experimentation (Boote et al. 2010; Kersebaum et al. 2015; Lobell et al. 2009). Such models are also helpful to scale up impacts from local (field experimentation) to landscape and regional levels (Duru et al. 2015). In this context, the main goal of this study is to review the extent to which agroecosystem models have been applied to (1) understand and design new arrangements of crops to increase crop diversity at the field and landscape scale by considering natural field heterogeneities in various soils; (2) quantify the effects of new arrangements of crops on resource use efficiency, ESS, and biodiversity; and (3) to specify requirements of models needed to be useful for these applications. 2 Methodology In a first step, the definitions of the scales of crop diversification were defined from available public…

fetched_contents.text: DSSAT Overview About DSSAT The Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) is a windows-based software application program that comprises crop simulation models for over 45 crops (as of Version 4.8.5) as well as tools to facilitate effective use of the models. The tools include database management programs for soil, weather, crop management and experimental data, utilities, and application programs. The crop simulation models simulate growth, development and yield as a function of the soil-plant-atmosphere dynamics. DSSAT and its crop simulation models have been used for a wide range of applications at different spatial and temporal scales. This includes on-farm and precision management, regional assessments of the impact of climate variability and climate change, gene-based modeling and breeding selection, crop water use, greenhouse gas emissions, climate smart agriculture, bioenergy, agrivoltaics, and long-term sustainability through the soil organic carbon and nitrogen balances. DSSAT has been used by more than 30,000 researchers, educators, consultants, extension agents, growers, and policy and decision makers in over 198 countries worldwide. The crop models require daily weather data, soil surface and profile information, and detailed crop management as input. Crop genetic information is defined in a crop species file that is provided by DSSAT, while cultivar or variety information that should be provided by the user. Simulations are initiated either at planting or prior to planting through the simulation of a bare fallow period. These simulations are conducted at a daily step or in some cases, at an hourly time step depending on the process and the crop model. At the end of each day, the plant and soil water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon balances are updated, as well as the crop’s vegetative and reproductive development stage. For applications, DSSAT combines crop, soil, and weather data bases with crop models and application programs to simulate multi-year outcomes of crop management strategies. DSSAT integrates the effects of soil, crop phenotype, weather and management options, and allows users to ask “what if” questions by conducting virtual simulation experiments on a desktop computer in minutes which would consume a significant part of an agronomist’s career if conducted as real experiments. DSSAT also provides tools for evaluation of crop model outputs with experimental data, thus allowing users to compare simulated outcomes with observed results. This is critical prior to any application of a crop model, especially if real-world decisions or recommendations are based on modeled results. Crop model evaluation is accomplished by inputting the user’s minimum data, running the model, and comparing outputs with observed data. By simulating probable outcomes of crop management strategies, DSSAT offers users information with which to rapidly appraise new crops, products, and practices for adoption. With the release of DSSAT v4.7, many changes have been incorporated — from both the structure of the crop models and the interface to the models and associated analysis and utility programs. DSSAT v4.8.0 was released in 2021 with further improvements and changes as well as models for new crops. The latest DSSAT v4.8.5 was released in December, 2024 with additional improvements and changes. The DSSAT package provides models of 45 crops with new tools that facilitate the creation and management of experimental, soil, and weather data files. DSSAT v4.8.5 also includes improved application programs for seasonal, spatial, climate change, in-season yield forecasting, and sequence and crop rotation analyses that assess the economic risks and environmental impacts associated with irrigation, fertilizer and nutrient management, climate variability, climate change, soil carbon sequestration, and precision management. “DSSAT 2021 Update” The following presentation entitled “Improvement and Application of Agroecosystem Models: The DSSAT experience” was presented by Gerrit Hoogenboom during the Symposium – “Improvement and Application of Crop Growth and Agroecosystem Models for Knowledge Advancement and Sustainable Development” as part of the 2021 ASA-CSSA-SSSA Annual Meeting held in Salt Lake City, Utah, USA “DSSAT is a vision” Following presentation was made at the 2011 American Society of Agronomy Meeting in San Antonio, Texas, by Dr. Gerrit Hoogenboom – at a special oral symposium “Honoring James Jones: Agroclimatology and Agronomic Modeling“.

fetched_contents.text: Bayesian calibration and uncertainty analysis of an agroecosystem model under different N management practices Introduction The agroecosystem model describes the multiple processes and their interactions of the cropland ecosystem, involving various soil and crop processes, including soil water movement, soil N transport and transformation, soil heat transfer, soil organic matter turnover, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop growth (Parton et al., 1998, Hansen et al., 2012, Li et al., 2000). Agroecosystem models, such as DAISY (Hansen et al., 2012), DNDC (Li et al., 2000), RZWQM (Ma et al., 2012), DAYCENT (Parton et al., 1998), WNMM (Li et al., 2007), and WHCNS (Liang et al., 2016), provide powerful tools to evaluate the effects of various field management practices on soil water and N fates, as well as crop growth in cropland ecosystems; thus, they are widely used in crop yield prediction, water and N flux simulation, environmental impact assessment, and exploring best management practices (BMPs) under various soil, climate, and field management conditions (Hansen et al., 2012, Coucheney et al., 2015, Huang et al., 2020). These models play a key role in understanding and analyzing agroecosystem processes. Soil water heat carbon nitrogen simulator (WHCNS) is a process-based agroecosystem model, which has shown good performance in simulating soil water movement, water balances, N fates, and crop growth for summer wheat-summer maize, spring maize, rice, and vegetable cropping systems under different field management practices (irrigation, fertilization, manure, mulching, crop rotation, tillage, etc.) in China (Li et al., 2015a, Liang et al., 2016, Liang et al., 2018, Liang et al., 2019, Shi et al., 2020, Chen et al., 2020). At present, this model has been used in optimizing water and N management practices in various cropland ecosystems (Liang et al., 2016, Liang et al., 2021, Shi et al., 2020), predicting crop yield, soil water balance, N leaching at the regional scale (Chen et al., 2020, Chen et al., 2021), modeling N leaching and crop yield under changing climate (He et al., 2018), and assessing water and N footprint of alterative cropping system (Xu et al., 2020). Many key soil and crop processes in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum, including soil water movement, soil N transformation and transport, soil organic turnover, soil heat transfer, and crop growth, are described in the WHCNS model, which require many input parameters. Parameter calibration of the model is usually time-consuming and it holds great uncertainty in model simulations, particularly for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil (Yang et al., 2014, Jabloun et al., 2018, Gurung et al., 2020). To improve model calibration efficiency and reduce model uncertainty, several studies proposed the two-step method by integrating global sensitivity analysis (GSA) and Bayesian techniques (Esmaeil et al., 2014, Jin et al., 2018). Sensitivity analysis is regarded as the first step to identify sensitive parameters and reduce parameter estimation efficiency before conducting Bayesian calibration. The method shows high calibration efficiency and simulation accuracy for process-based models. Founded in Esmaeil et al. (2014) and Jin et al. (2018), the model calibration efficiency and performance of RZWQM and AquaCrop models were greatly improved by using this two-step method. Many parameter estimation algorithms were developed based on Bayesian techniques, such as generalized likelihood uncertainty estimation (GLUE), Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and Different Evolution Adaptive Metropolis (DREAM), which can be used to quantify different sources of model uncertainties and estimate the posterior distribution of model input parameters (Vrugt and ter Braak, 2011, Seidel et al., 2018). The DREAM algorithm is an improved version of classical MCMC sampling methods by increasing sampling efficiencies in high-dimensional search spaces, which have advantages to deal with issues with high-dimensionality, nonlinearity, and local optima (Vrugt et al., 2008, Dumont et al., 2014, Vrugt, 2016). Thus, it provides a robust estimation of parameter posterior distributions (Zhang et al., 2020). The DREAM has been successfully used in estimating model input parameters of process-based hydrology models (Vrugt et al., 2008, Joseph and Guillaume, 2013), atmospheric chemistry models (Partridge et al., 2012), crop models (Dumont et al., 2014, Sexton et al., 2016, Gao et al., 2020), and agroecosystem models (Myrgiotis et al., 2018, Zhang et al., 2020). For agroecosystem models, few studies comprehensively evaluated the performance of the DREAM algorithm using long-term time observation data, and the effects of different N management practices on simulation uncertainties remain unclear. Thus, in this study, the DREAM method was selected to estimate model input parameter and analyze model uncertainty of the WHCNS model. This study aimed to (i) identify the sensitive parameters of the WHCNS model under different N management practices based on GSA, (ii) estimate the posterior distribution of the sensitive parameters using the DREAM algorithm, and (iii) analyze the parameter uncertainties in simulating soil water content, soil N dynamics, and crop growth under different N management practices. fetched_contents.text: Adapting an agroecosystem model to account for cover crop management in the Midwest USA 1. Introduction Cover crops are widely touted for their potential to ‘perennialize’ annual cropping systems that are inherently “leaky”, meaning they tend to lose carbon [1], water [2,3], and nutrients [4,5]. Cover crops have the potential to improve soil health [6,7], reduce greenhouse gas emissions [8], and reduce leaching and runoff [9], while maintaining or even improving crop yields in agricultural systems [10]. The effectiveness of cover crops in restoring these ecosystem functions hinges on their successful establishment and abundant growth during periods when conditions for germination and growth can be quite harsh, depending on geography and climate [11,12]. In the Upper Midwest USA, where maize (Zea mays L.) and soybean (Glycine max L.) cover approximately 75 % of the agricultural landscape, soil and nutrient loss and declining water quality have led to steady increases in cover cropped acreage [13]. While cover crops offer potential benefits, their widespread adoption remains limited [13]. Several factors contribute to this, including challenges in choosing the right species, limited time for establishment after fall harvest, and concerns about potential yield reductions in the main crop [[14], [15], [16]]. Numerical simulation models can be used to evaluate the efficacy and impact of cover crops on agroecosystem processes under a range of environmental and management conditions. Numerous studies have modeled the effect of cover crops focusing on nitrate leaching reductions [[17], [18], [19], [20]]. Additionally, researchers have used process-based models to evaluate cover crop biomass as well as the impact of cover crops on maize yields [21,22] and emissions [23,24]. These studies have provided valuable insights using a variety of models (APSIM, DNDCv.CAN, RZWQM2, DayCent, RyeGro, STICS), each with its own strengths and weaknesses. While Agro-IBIS has not previously been used to simulate cover crops, we selected it for further advancement due to its demonstrated robustness in modeling a wide range in Midwestern agroecosystems (e.g. corn, soybean, wheat, miscanthus, switchgrass) and previous success in addressing interdisciplinary studies of food-energy-water systems as part of multi-model efforts with other collaborators [[25], [26], [27], [28]]. Furthermore, Agro-IBIS is a well-established process-based model that integrates plant growth, eco-physiology, soil-water dynamics, biogeochemical processes, and solute transport at high spatial and temporal resolutions. Its underlying framework and representation of a diversity of plant functional types makes it well suited for extending its capacity to include cover crops. Agro-IBIS and IBIS have also been employed to predict maize yield [29] and nitrate losses from agroecosystems [30,31], ecosystem functions in perennial grasslands [32], vegetation phenology [33], surface energy fluxes [[34], [35], [36], [37]], water balance [[38], [39], [40], [41]], and water quality [42,43]. In this study, we modified the Agro-IBIS model's winter wheat plant functional type (PFT) to represent winter cereal rye, a cool-season winter annual grass cover crop along with its management. We evaluated the revised model by comparing simulated aboveground biomass (AGB) to observed AGB data from winter cereal rye cover crop experiments conducted in continuous maize and maize-soybean rotations in southern Wisconsin. Additionally, the impact of key environmental factors on both observed and simulated AGB of winter cereal rye cover crop was used as another indicator of the model's successful validation. 2. Methods 2.1. Study region Our study region was the University of Wisconsin-Madison's Arlington Agricultural Research Station (AARS; 43.3012 N, 89.3467 W) located in southern Wisconsin's Columbia County, which is characterized by warm, humid summers, and cold winters. Based on 1991–2020 climatology (NOAA, 2023), Arlington receives average annual precipitation of 902 mm, with typical snowfall of 1069 mm. July is the hottest and most humid month of the year with an average daily high temperature of 27.9 °C with 60 % humidity. January is the coldest and driest month of the year with an average nighttime minimum temperature of −12.9 °C and 31 mm of precipitation. Summer (Jun-Aug) is the wettest period with 37 % of annual precipitation, while winter (Dec-Feb) is the driest period receiving only 11.5 % of annual precipitation. The predominant soil series at Arlington, WI, is Plano silt loam, which consists of very deep and well drained soils classified as fine-silty, mixed, superactive, mesic Typic Argiudolls. Slopes at AARS range from 0 % to 2 %. 2.2. Field study Field data from several studies incorporating winter cereal rye cover crops at AARS between 2004 and 2021 (unpublished data) were compiled to compare with Agro-IBIS output. In all these studies, winter cereal rye was planted as a cover crop in continuous maize (2005 to 2007, 2013 to 2019, and 2021) or maize-soybean rotations (2013 to 2017 and 2021) following harvest of the grain crop in the late summer or fall of each year. Depending on the field study and treatment, maize was harvested for silage, grain only, or grain and stover, with the end-use of the maize crop (e.g., silage vs. grain) determining the harvest date for the main crop and the subsequent planting date for the winter cereal rye. Winter cereal rye was typically planted between September and November following maize. When winter cereal rye followed soybean in the maize-soybean rotation system, it was typically planted in early- to mid-October. Winter cereal rye was terminated between the end of April and early June prior to, or just after, planting the main crop (maize or soybean). Spatial representation and computational methods

Agroecosystem models suitable for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale typically represent field geometry, patches, and spatial heterogeneity through discretized landscape grids or patch-based structures. The evidence here shows that spatial simulation models often use grid-cell or tract-based structures, where patches or land-use classes are potential locations for areal land-use change, and landscape patterns are represented by nested grid structures with highlighted patches [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This is important for crop diversification because it allows the model to capture spatially differentiated management zones, such as cropland patches, grassland patches, or heterogeneous field units, which are essential for allocating different crops, cover crops, or diverse field arrangements [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The evidence also suggests that spatial representations can be linked to landscape dynamics, including land-use change and land-use pattern shifts over time [N2-R4], which matters for diversification because management decisions often depend on neighboring land uses and landscape structure.

Which spatial discretization methods are used and when they matter? The evidence points to grid-based landscape representation as a central method, with patches and grid cells serving as the basic spatial units [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also references a spatial simulation model that predicts temporal changes in land-use patterns in a Piedmont county, with five land-use categories used for simulation [N2-R4]. In such models, spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns influence diversification outcomes because the model can represent transitions between land-use states and the effects of landscape structure on resource allocation and ecological interactions [N2-R4]. The evidence also indicates that spatial models can use stand-age maps as input, where grid-cell values represent age, and then produce new land-use states over time [N2-R5]. This matters for diversification because the spatial arrangement of crop and non-crop elements affects pest regulation, biodiversity, and resource use efficiency [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. In other words, when the model needs to simulate landscape-level feedbacks such as edge effects, patch adjacency, or heterogeneous resource distribution, grid-cell or patch-based methods become computationally relevant [N2-R2][N2-R3].

How spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns influence diversification outcomes? The evidence supports the idea that spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns can affect diversification outcomes through nested grid structures and land-use pattern dynamics [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The same evidence also notes that smaller field sizes or patches are associated with multiple benefits to ecosystems, especially biodiversity and species richness, and that diversified landscapes via smaller patches and additional landscape elements such as hedgerows or flower strips promote farmland biodiversity and pest regulation [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This means that, in a field-scale model, spatial feedbacks can emerge from the interaction between crop patches, cover crops, field boundaries, and surrounding non-crop vegetation strips, which together influence pest dynamics, pollination, and resource competition [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Therefore, spatial representation matters most when the model is intended to simulate the coexistence of diverse crop species, management zones, and landscape elements, and when the goal is to capture how landscape pattern affects diversification benefits rather than only aggregate yield or soil properties [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

Overall, the model architecture for spatial crop diversification at field scale relies on grid-cell or patch-based discretization, with landscape-level feedbacks captured through land-use change rules and spatial structure [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The strongest implications are that the model must represent patches, heterogeneity, and landscape context, and that spatial resolution and representation matter most when the diversification strategy depends on spatial arrangement rather than uniform management [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].
node_outputs.N7:
Model architecture and functional components supporting diversification

To simulate crop diversification at the field scale, agroecosystem models need compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management, along with mechanisms to represent species interactions, resource competition, and decision rules for crop sequence and spatial allocation. The evidence provided here indicates that agroecosystem models simulate crop growth and development in response to environmental conditions and management practices, including radiation, temperature, water availability, atmospheric CO2, and nutrient availability from soils, and that they incorporate crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other management decisions [N1-F1]. This is directly relevant because diversification requires modeling not only the growth of individual crops but also how they interact with other crops, soil, pests, and management choices.

What model compartments are needed to represent crops, soils, pests, and management? The evidence points to a broad compartmental structure: crop species/cultivars, soil processes, biotic interactions, and management practices. The review explicitly states that agroecosystem models simulate crop growth and development and soil processes in response to environmental conditions and management practices [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that crop diversification is the deliberate introduction of multiple crop species, varieties, and management practices within agricultural systems [N1-R3]. In addition, the same review notes that agroecosystem management can increase beneficial biotic interactions, improve pest management, and decrease reliance on external inputs [N1-R2]. This means that the model must include compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management, and that pest management is especially important for diversification because it can be improved by increasing beneficial biotic interactions [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The evidence also supports the inclusion of cover crops and crop rotations as management strategies, with the review noting that cover crops grown in rotation with cash crops are a realistic strategy to increase agroecosystem diversity [N5-R2]. This implies that management compartments should also include crop rotation, cover crop management, and other diversification practices [N5-R2].

How species interactions and resource competition are modeled? The evidence indicates that agroecosystem models can capture species interactions and competition through biotic interactions, pest dynamics, and resource use efficiency. The review states that spatial and temporal crop diversification can improve resource use efficiency because resources can be allocated according to specific field characteristics [N1-F1]. It also notes that crop diversification improves soil fertility and structure, crop yield, yield stability, nitrogen cycling, carbon sequestration, pest control, biodiversity, and reduced yield risk [N1-F1]. In addition, the review explicitly links crop diversification to improved pest regulation and biodiversity [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that species interactions and resource competition are modeled through pest regulation, competition for nutrients and water, and the broader ecological effects of diversification. The evidence also supports the idea that cover crops can modify the microenvironment and competition among crops [N5-R2], which matters for diversification because it changes the resource landscape and plant-soil feedbacks [N5-R2]. In short, the model must represent how crop species interact with each other and with pests, how they compete for resources, and how management practices alter these interactions [N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-R2].

What management rules or decision rules govern crop sequence and spatial allocation? The evidence shows that management rules and decision rules are central to diversification design. The review states that agroecosystem models are used to understand and design new crop arrangements at field and landscape scale, and that they are useful for quantifying the effects of new crop arrangements on resource use efficiency and ecosystem services [N1-F1]. It also notes that field classification into smaller units based on soil heterogeneities is required for site-specific management [N1-F1]. This implies that the model must include decision rules or management rules that determine how crops are sequenced over time and how they are allocated across space. The evidence also supports crop rotation and cover crop management as decision rules, with crop rotation providing higher diversity over time and cover crops offering potential to improve yield and soil health [N1-R4][N5-R2]. Furthermore, the review mentions that management practices such as crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other practices are part of agroecosystem models [N1-F1]. These management rules are important because they govern the sequence of crops and the spatial distribution of crop types within a field. The evidence also indicates that the model must account for how management decisions are made in response to soil heterogeneity and field structure [N1-F1].

Taken together, the model architecture needed to support diversification includes crop compartments, soil compartments, pest compartments, and management compartments; it must represent species interactions and resource competition through biotic interactions, pest regulation, and nutrient/water competition; and it must include decision rules or management rules that determine crop sequence and spatial allocation [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R2]. The strongest conclusion is that diversification simulation at the field scale requires a compartmentalized model that integrates crop identity, soil state, pest dynamics, and management decisions, with explicit rules governing how crops are sequenced and where they are placed in the landscape [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R2].
node_outputs.N10:
Field-scale validity and practical constraints

Agroecosystem models are useful for field-scale diversification, but their performance and practical constraints are important. The evidence suggests that field-scale validity is constrained by the need for calibration, validation, and uncertainty analysis. The Bayesian calibration and uncertainty analysis study explicitly states that model calibration is time-consuming and holds great uncertainty in model simulations, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. It also notes that several studies proposed a two-step method integrating global sensitivity analysis and Bayesian techniques to improve model calibration efficiency and reduce uncertainty [N4-F3]. This matters for field-scale application because the model must be calibrated against field data, and calibration uncertainty can be large if the model is complex and the data are sparse [N4-F3].

How well does the model perform at the field scale versus larger scales? The evidence indicates that field-scale models are part of a broader modeling hierarchy, but they are often calibrated and validated against field data while also being used to upscale to landscape and regional scales [N4-F3][N1-F1]. The DSSAT overview says that DSSAT combines crop, soil, and weather databases with crop models to simulate multi-year outcomes of crop management strategies, and that it can be used at on-farm, precision management, regional, and long-term sustainability scales [N3-F4]. This implies that field-scale models can be valid at the field scale, but their utility depends on the scale of the question being asked. The review on crop diversification design also emphasizes that agroecosystem models are useful for field and landscape-scale applications, especially when they incorporate natural field heterogeneities and site-specific management [N1-F1]. So the model can perform well at the field scale when it is calibrated to local data and validated against field observations, but its larger-scale validity depends on whether the model can represent aggregated processes without losing local detail [N4-F3][N1-F1].

Calibration and validation practices specific to diversification? The evidence shows that calibration and validation are central to model reliability. The review on calibration and validation states that model prediction error is defined as the uncertainty in a model's prediction as determined from comparison to measurements, and that experimental field data are used at different levels of complexity to calibrate, validate, and improve agroecosystem models [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The Bayesian calibration study adds that parameter calibration is usually time-consuming and that uncertainty analysis is needed because of high model complexity [N4-F3]. For diversification specifically, the model must be calibrated against field data on crop growth, soil properties, management inputs, and possibly pest or yield outcomes [N4-R3][N4-F3]. The evidence also implies that validation practices should include comparison with observed data across multiple field conditions and management scenarios, because the same study notes that model evaluation is accomplished by inputting the user’s minimum data, running the model, and comparing outputs with observed data [N3-F4]. This is especially important for diversification because management sequences and spatial allocations can vary widely, and the model must be validated under those diverse conditions [N4-R2][N4-R3][N3-F4].

Major uncertainties and limitations for real-world application? The evidence identifies several major uncertainties and limitations. First, calibration uncertainty is high because of model complexity, especially in soil and crop processes [N4-F3]. Second, the need for field data limits the model’s applicability where data are sparse or expensive to collect [N4-R3][N4-R4]. Third, the review on field-scale experiments notes that one of the greatest limitations to field-scale experimentation is a dearth of acceptable methods for design and statistical evaluation, and that experimental error remains an important concern [N6-R2]. This matters because, even if the model is validated against some field data, the uncertainty from experimental design and measurement error can reduce confidence in real-world application [N6-R2]. Fourth, the review on agricultural system data and models emphasizes the need to understand current capabilities and limitations of agricultural systems models, suggesting that model limitations are not just technical but also practical and data-dependent [N6-R5]. In the context of diversification, the main limitations include uncertainty in parameter estimates, dependence on field data availability, and the difficulty of designing field experiments that can fully test model behavior under diverse management and environmental conditions [N4-F3][N4-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, the field-scale validity of agroecosystem models for diversification depends on strong calibration and validation against field data, but practical constraints include high calibration uncertainty, limited data availability, and methodological limitations in field experimentation [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The strongest conclusion is that the model is most useful at the field scale when it is well-calibrated, validated against local conditions, and used with caution about uncertainty, especially in complex soil and management contexts [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3].

Temporal representation and process dynamics

Agroecosystem models suitable for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale must capture seasonal, annual, and longer-term dynamics. The evidence shows that these models are often built on daily time steps, and in some cases hourly time steps, depending on the process and crop model [N3-F4]. DSSAT, as a representative agroecosystem model, simulates growth, development, and yield as a function of soil-plant-atmosphere dynamics, and it conducts simulations at a daily step or in some cases at an hourly time step [N3-F4]. This temporal structure is important for crop diversification because crop rotation, cover crops, and management sequences are typically studied over seasons and years [N3-R3][N5-F2]. The review on crop diversification also states that agroecosystem models are used to understand and design new crop arrangements at field and landscape scale, and that they are useful for quantifying effects over time [N1-F1]. This implies that the model should not treat diversification as a one-off decision but as a dynamic process that evolves across seasons and years.

What time steps are used and how they affect crop diversification realism? The evidence points to daily time steps as the standard in many agroecosystem models, with some models using hourly time steps when needed [N3-F4]. The DSSAT overview explicitly states that simulations are conducted at a daily step or in some cases at an hourly time step depending on the process and the crop model [N3-F4]. This matters for diversification realism because daily steps are sufficient to capture growth and development stages, while hourly steps can improve accuracy for processes such as water and nutrient uptake [N3-F4]. For crop diversification, the time step choice affects the ability to simulate crop rotation, cover crop establishment, and management transitions. The review notes that crop rotation is an important management practice and that agroecosystem models can be used to simulate crop rotation [N3-R3], and the cover crop study shows that cover crops are managed across periods with harsh conditions after harvest, with planting and termination dates influencing performance [N5-F2]. Therefore, a fine time step is important when the model must capture planting, growth, termination, and residue effects over the growing season [N3-F4][N5-F2].

How transitions between crop states and disturbances are modeled? The evidence indicates that transitions between crop states and disturbances are modeled through crop growth and development stages, soil-water and nutrient balances, and management decisions. DSSAT updates plant and soil water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon balances at the end of each day, and it also updates crop vegetative and reproductive development stages [N3-F4]. This means that the model captures transitions between crop states implicitly through growth stages, rather than as abrupt switches. The cover crop study further shows that winter cereal rye is planted after harvest and terminated before planting the main crop, with interseeding used to extend the growing season [N5-F2]. This suggests that disturbance transitions, such as harvest, planting, and termination, are modeled as management events rather than purely environmental disturbances [N5-F2]. The DSSAT overview also states that the model allows users to ask “what if” questions by conducting virtual simulation experiments, which implies that management transitions can be tested dynamically [N3-F4]. In addition, the review on crop diversification emphasizes that agroecosystem models can be used to quantify the effects of new crop arrangements over time, including multi-year outcomes of management strategies [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that transitions are not modeled only at the crop level but also across years and management sequences [N1-F1].

Overall, the temporal representation needed for crop diversification at the field scale is daily or hourly time steps, depending on process detail [N3-F4]. This allows the model to capture seasonal and annual dynamics, crop growth stages, and management transitions [N3-F4][N5-F2]. The evidence also shows that transitions between crop states and disturbances are modeled through growth stages, soil balances, and management events [N3-F4][N5-F2]. The strongest conclusion is that a fine temporal resolution improves realism for diversification, especially when the model must simulate crop rotation, cover crops, and management sequences over time [N3-F4][N5-F2][N1-F1].

Data requirements and model design constraints

Field-scale agroecosystem models require specific data for calibration and scenario design, and model complexity and parameterization scale with data availability. The evidence shows that experimental field data are used at different levels of complexity to calibrate, validate, and improve agroecosystem models [N4-R3]. The Bayesian calibration study further states that model calibration is usually time-consuming and holds great uncertainty, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. This means that the model’s data requirements are not just minimal; they must include enough detail to support parameter estimation and uncertainty reduction. The DSSAT overview says that crop models require daily weather data, soil surface and profile information, and detailed crop management as input [N3-F4]. This is especially important for field-scale applications because the model must be informed by local conditions, not only averaged regional data.

What field-scale data are needed for calibration and scenario design? The evidence points to a range of field-scale data: daily weather data, soil surface and profile information, detailed crop management, crop genetic information, cultivar or variety information, and experimental data for evaluation [N3-F4][N4-R3]. The calibration and validation guidance notes that model prediction error is defined as the uncertainty in a model's prediction as determined from comparison to measurements, and that experimental field data are used at different levels of complexity [N4-R2][N4-R3]. This suggests that calibration requires not only yield or biomass data but also process-level data such as soil moisture, nitrogen dynamics, and growth stages [N3-F4][N4-R3]. The cover crop study adds that numerical simulation models can evaluate the efficacy and impact of cover crops under a range of environmental and management conditions, and that the model was validated against observed aboveground biomass data from winter cereal rye cover crop experiments [N5-F2]. This indicates that scenario design needs management-specific data, including planting and termination dates, seeding rates, and crop rotations [N5-F2]. Overall, the model requires weather, soil, crop genetics, management, and process observations to be calibrated and validated at the field scale [N3-F4][N4-R3][N4-R2][N5-F2].

How model complexity and parameterization scale with data availability? The evidence shows that more complex models require more data and are more uncertain when data are sparse. The Bayesian calibration study states that parameter calibration is usually time-consuming and holds great uncertainty in model simulations, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. It also notes that sensitivity analysis and Bayesian techniques are used to improve calibration efficiency and reduce uncertainty [N4-F3]. This means that as the model becomes more complex—adding soil-water dynamics, nitrogen cycling, pest interactions, and cover crop management—the required data set also expands. The review on agricultural systems data and models notes that the current state of agricultural systems science focuses on the capabilities and limitations of agricultural systems models, implying that model complexity increases the need for comprehensive data [N6-R5]. In practice, when data are abundant, the model can be calibrated more precisely and validated against multiple data sources; when data are limited, the model must be simpler, parameter estimates are less certain, and the risk of overfitting increases [N4-F3][N6-R5].

Constraints on spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and management detail. The evidence supports that spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and management detail are tightly linked to model design constraints. The review on crop diversification design notes that field classification into smaller units considering soil heterogeneities is required for site-specific management [N1-F1]. This suggests that spatial resolution must be sufficient to represent heterogeneous fields, but higher resolution also increases computational demand and data requirements [N1-F1]. The temporal constraint is daily or hourly time steps, depending on the process and crop model [N3-F4]. This means that finer temporal resolution improves realism but may require more detailed weather and management data [N3-F4]. For management detail, the evidence shows that crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other management practices are part of agroecosystem models [N1-F1]. The cover crop study explicitly states that the model was adapted to cover crop management, including planting and termination dates, and that it was evaluated against observed biomass data from cover crop experiments [N5-F2]. This implies that management detail must be sufficiently granular to capture crop rotation, cover crop sequences, and other diversification practices [N5-F2]. 

The major constraints are therefore: spatial resolution must match field heterogeneity without excessive computational burden, temporal resolution must be fine enough to capture growth and management transitions but may be constrained by data availability, and management detail must be detailed enough to represent crop diversification strategies such as crop rotation and cover crops, but that detail can increase parameterization complexity and data demand [N1-F1][N3-F4][N5-F2]. The strongest conclusion is that field-scale agroecosystem models require rich weather, soil, crop, and management data for calibration and validation, and that model complexity and parameterization scale upward with data availability, while spatial and temporal resolution and management detail impose practical design constraints [N3-F4][N4-R3][N4-F3][N1-F1][N5-F2].

## Key features of agroecosystem models that make them suitable for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale

Agroecosystem models are well suited for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale because they combine a broad set of model compartments with spatial and temporal process dynamics, while also being calibrated and validated against field data. Across the five branch reports, the evidence consistently supports the same conclusion: these models are powerful tools for understanding how crop diversity, management, and landscape structure interact over time and space [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F4][N4-F3][N5-F2].

---

## 1) Model architecture: compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management

A field-scale agroecosystem model must include compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management to represent the full system of crop diversification. The evidence shows that agroecosystem models simulate crop growth and development in response to environmental conditions and management practices, including radiation, temperature, water availability, atmospheric CO2, and nutrient availability from soils [N1-F1]. They also include crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other management decisions [N1-F1].

For diversification, the model must also explicitly represent pest dynamics and beneficial biotic interactions. The review notes that agroecosystem management can increase beneficial biotic interactions and improve pest management, while decreasing reliance on external inputs [N1-R2]. This is especially important because crop diversification often aims to reduce pest pressure and improve biodiversity [N1-F1][N5-R2]. The same branch report also explicitly links crop diversification to improved pest regulation and biodiversity [N1-F1], showing that the model architecture must capture both competition among species and the ecological benefits of diversity.

In addition, the evidence supports the inclusion of cover crops and crop rotations as management strategies. Cover crops grown in rotation with cash crops are described as a realistic strategy to increase agroecosystem diversity [N5-R2], and crop rotation is noted as an important management practice that agroecosystem models can simulate [N3-R3]. These findings mean the model architecture must include decision rules or management rules that govern crop sequence and spatial allocation [N1-F1][N5-R2].

---

## 2) Species interactions and resource competition

The evidence shows that agroecosystem models are designed to represent species interactions and resource competition. The review states that spatial and temporal crop diversification improves resource use efficiency because resources can be allocated according to specific field characteristics [N1-F1]. It also notes that crop diversification improves soil fertility and structure, crop yield, yield stability, nitrogen cycling, carbon sequestration, pest control, biodiversity, and reduced yield risk [N1-F1]. These outcomes imply that the model must represent competition for nutrients and water, as well as interactions among crops and between crops and pests.

The evidence further indicates that cover crops can modify the microenvironment and competition among crops [N5-R2]. This means that the model should not treat crops as isolated entities; instead, it should represent how different crop species interact through shared resources and how management changes these interactions [N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-R2]. The branch report on crop diversification design also emphasizes that agroecosystem models are used to understand and design new crop arrangements at field and landscape scale, and that they are useful for quantifying the effects of new crop arrangements on resource use efficiency and ecosystem services [N1-F1]. This is a key feature for field-scale diversification because it allows the model to evaluate whether a given diversification strategy actually improves ecological performance.

---

## 3) Spatial representation: field geometry, patches, and landscape patterns

Agroecosystem models suitable for field-scale diversification use spatial discretization methods that can represent field geometry, patches, and spatial heterogeneity. The evidence points to grid-cell or patch-based structures, with patches and grid cells serving as the basic spatial units [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also references a spatial simulation model that predicts temporal changes in land-use patterns, with five land-use categories used for simulation [N2-R4]. This is important because crop diversification is often about allocating different crops, cover crops, or management zones across the field rather than treating the field as a uniform unit.

The evidence further shows that spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns influence diversification outcomes. The same branch report notes that nested grid structures and land-use pattern dynamics are central to spatial simulation [N2-R2][N2-R4], and that smaller field sizes or patches are associated with multiple benefits to ecosystems, especially biodiversity and species richness [N2-R5]. It also notes that diversified landscapes via smaller patches and additional landscape elements such as hedgerows or flower strips promote farmland biodiversity and pest regulation [N2-R5]. This means that spatial representation matters when the model is intended to simulate the coexistence of diverse crop species, management zones, and landscape elements, and when the goal is to capture how landscape pattern affects diversification benefits [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

In other words, the model should represent the field as a heterogeneous landscape made up of patches or management zones, and it should capture how those zones interact through spatial feedbacks such as edge effects, patch adjacency, and landscape structure [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This is especially important for crop diversification because management decisions often depend on neighboring land uses and landscape context [N2-R4].

---

## 4) Temporal representation: daily or hourly time steps and process dynamics

Agroecosystem models suitable for field-scale crop diversification must capture seasonal, annual, and longer-term dynamics. The evidence shows that many agroecosystem models use daily time steps, and in some cases hourly time steps, depending on the process and the crop model [N3-F4]. DSSAT is explicitly described as simulating growth, development, and yield as a function of soil-plant-atmosphere dynamics, and it conducts simulations at a daily step or in some cases at an hourly time step [N3-F4]. This temporal structure is important because crop rotation, cover crops, and management sequences are typically studied over seasons and years [N3-R3][N5-F2].

The evidence also shows that transitions between crop states and disturbances are modeled through growth stages, soil-water and nutrient balances, and management decisions. DSSAT updates plant and soil water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and carbon balances at the end of each day, and it also updates crop vegetative and reproductive development stages [N3-F4]. This means that transitions between crop states are not modeled as abrupt switches but as implicit developmental transitions. The cover crop study further shows that winter cereal rye is planted after harvest and terminated before planting the main crop, with interseeding used to extend the growing season [N5-F2]. This suggests that disturbance transitions, such as harvest, planting, and termination, are modeled as management events rather than purely environmental disturbances [N5-F2].

The review on crop diversification design also emphasizes that agroecosystem models are used to understand and design new crop arrangements at field and landscape scale, and that they are useful for quantifying effects over time [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that temporal representation is not just about weather or yield, but about the dynamic evolution of diversification strategies over the crop cycle and across years [N1-F1][N3-F4][N5-F2].

---

## 5) Calibration, validation, and uncertainty analysis

Field-scale validity depends heavily on calibration and validation. The evidence shows that model calibration is usually time-consuming and holds great uncertainty in model simulations, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. It also notes that several studies proposed a two-step method integrating global sensitivity analysis and Bayesian techniques to improve calibration efficiency and reduce uncertainty [N4-F3]. This is central to field-scale application because the model must be calibrated against field data, and uncertainty analysis is needed to assess confidence in the results [N4-R2][N4-R3].

The branch report on field-scale validity and practical constraints states that experimental field data are used at different levels of complexity to calibrate, validate, and improve agroecosystem models [N4-R3]. The DSSAT overview adds that crop models require daily weather data, soil surface and profile information, and detailed crop management as input, and that model evaluation is accomplished by inputting the user’s minimum data, running the model, and comparing outputs with observed data [N3-F4]. This means that validation practices must include comparison with observed data across multiple field conditions and management scenarios, because the same study notes that model prediction error is defined as the uncertainty in a model’s prediction as determined from comparison to measurements [N4-R2][N4-R3].

For diversification specifically, the model must be validated under diverse management and environmental conditions. The review on field-scale experiments notes that one of the greatest limitations to field-scale experimentation is a dearth of acceptable methods for design and statistical evaluation, and that experimental error remains an important concern [N6-R2]. This means that even if the model is validated against some field data, uncertainty from experimental design and measurement error can reduce confidence in real-world application [N6-R2]. The review on agricultural system data and models also emphasizes the need to understand current capabilities and limitations of agricultural systems models [N6-R5].

---

## 6) Field-scale data requirements and design constraints

Field-scale agroecosystem models require rich data for calibration and scenario design. The evidence points to a range of field-scale data: daily weather data, soil surface and profile information, detailed crop management, crop genetic information, cultivar or variety information, and experimental data for evaluation [N3-F4][N4-R3]. The Bayesian calibration study further states that model calibration is usually time-consuming and holds great uncertainty, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. This means that the model’s data requirements are not just minimal; they must include enough detail to support parameter estimation and uncertainty reduction.

The evidence also shows that model complexity and parameterization scale with data availability. The Bayesian calibration study explicitly states that parameter calibration is usually time-consuming and holds great uncertainty in model simulations, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. It also notes that sensitivity analysis and Bayesian techniques are used to improve calibration efficiency and reduce uncertainty [N4-F3]. This means that as the model becomes more complex—adding soil-water dynamics, nitrogen cycling, pest interactions, and cover crop management—the required data set also expands [N4-F3][N6-R5]. When data are abundant, the model can be calibrated more precisely and validated against multiple data sources; when data are limited, the model must be simpler, parameter estimates are less certain, and the risk of overfitting increases [N4-F3][N6-R5].

Constraints on spatial resolution, temporal frequency, and management detail are also important. The review on crop diversification design notes that field classification into smaller units considering soil heterogeneities is required for site-specific management [N1-F1]. This suggests that spatial resolution must be sufficient to represent heterogeneous fields, but higher resolution also increases computational demand and data requirements [N1-F1]. The temporal constraint is daily or hourly time steps, depending on the process and crop model [N3-F4]. This means that finer temporal resolution improves realism but may require more detailed weather and management data [N3-F4]. For management detail, the evidence shows that crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other management practices are part of agroecosystem models [N1-F1]. The cover crop study explicitly states that the model was adapted to cover crop management, including planting and termination dates, and that it was evaluated against observed biomass data from cover crop experiments [N5-F2]. This implies that management detail must be sufficiently granular to capture crop rotation, cover crop sequences, and other diversification practices [N5-F2].

---

## 7) Practical limitations and field-scale validity

The evidence shows that agroecosystem models are useful at the field scale, but their performance and practical constraints are important. The branch report on field-scale validity and practical constraints states that model calibration is time-consuming and holds great uncertainty, especially for soil variable simulation, because of the high complexity of N transport and transformation processes in soil [N4-F3]. It also notes that calibration uncertainty is a major concern when the model is used for real-world application [N4-F3][N4-R3].

The evidence further suggests that field-scale models can be valid at the field scale when they are calibrated to local data and validated against field observations, but their larger-scale validity depends on whether the model can represent aggregated processes without losing local detail [N4-F3][N1-F1]. The DSSAT overview states that DSSAT combines crop, soil, and weather databases with crop models to simulate multi-year outcomes of crop management strategies, and that it can be used at on-farm, precision management, regional, and long-term sustainability scales [N3-F4]. This indicates that field-scale models can be valid at the field scale, but they are part of a broader modeling hierarchy and may need to be upscaled carefully [N3-F4][N1-F1].

Major uncertainties and limitations include calibration uncertainty, limited data availability, and methodological limitations in field experimentation [N4-F3][N4-R3][N6-R2][N6-R5]. These limitations are especially relevant for diversification because management sequences and spatial allocations can vary widely, and the model must be validated under those diverse conditions [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

---

## 8) Integrated conclusion: what makes agroecosystem models suitable for field-scale crop diversification?

The key features that make agroecosystem models suitable for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale are:

1. **A broad compartmental architecture** that includes crops, soils, pests, and management [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R2].  
2. **Explicit modeling of species interactions and resource competition** to capture pest regulation, biodiversity, and resource use efficiency [N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-R2].  
3. **Management rules and decision rules** that govern crop sequence and spatial allocation [N1-F1][N5-R2].  
4. **Spatial representation through patches and grid-cell methods** that can capture field geometry, heterogeneity, and landscape patterns [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].  
5. **Daily or hourly temporal resolution** that supports seasonal, annual, and longer-term dynamics [N3-F4][N5-F2].  
6. **Strong calibration and validation practices** that use field data at different levels of complexity [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F3].  
7. **A recognition of uncertainty and data limitations** that constrains model design and application [N4-F3][N6-R2][N6-R5].  

These features together make agroecosystem models well suited for field-scale crop diversification: they can represent the ecological and management complexity of diversified cropping systems, while also being calibrated and validated against local data so that their results are meaningful for real-world decision support [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-F4][N4-R3][N5-F2].

Spatial representation and computational methods

Agroecosystem models suitable for simulating spatial and temporal crop diversification at the field scale typically represent field geometry, patches, and spatial heterogeneity through discretized landscape grids or patch-based structures. The evidence here shows that spatial simulation models often use grid-cell or tract-based structures, where patches or land-use classes are potential locations for areal land-use change, and landscape patterns are represented by nested grid structures with highlighted patches [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This is important for crop diversification because it allows the model to capture spatially differentiated management zones, such as cropland patches, grassland patches, or heterogeneous field units, which are essential for allocating different crops, cover crops, or diverse field arrangements [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The evidence also suggests that spatial representations can be linked to landscape dynamics, including land-use change and land-use pattern shifts over time [N2-R4], which matters for diversification because management decisions often depend on neighboring land uses and landscape structure.

Which spatial discretization methods are used and when they matter? The evidence points to grid-based landscape representation as a central method, with patches and grid cells serving as the basic spatial units [N2-R2][N2-R3]. It also references a spatial simulation model that predicts temporal changes in land-use patterns in a Piedmont county, with five land-use categories used for simulation [N2-R4]. In such models, spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns influence diversification outcomes because the model can represent transitions between land-use states and the effects of landscape structure on resource allocation and ecological interactions [N2-R4]. The evidence also indicates that spatial models can use stand-age maps as input, where grid-cell values represent age, and then produce new land-use states over time [N2-R5]. This matters for diversification because the spatial arrangement of crop and non-crop elements affects pest regulation, biodiversity, and resource use efficiency [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. In other words, when the model needs to simulate landscape-level feedbacks such as edge effects, patch adjacency, or heterogeneous resource distribution, grid-cell or patch-based methods become computationally relevant [N2-R2][N2-R3].

How spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns influence diversification outcomes? The evidence supports the idea that spatial feedbacks and landscape patterns can affect diversification outcomes through nested grid structures and land-use pattern dynamics [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The same evidence also notes that smaller field sizes or patches are associated with multiple benefits to ecosystems, especially biodiversity and species richness, and that diversified landscapes via smaller patches and additional landscape elements such as hedgerows or flower strips promote farmland biodiversity and pest regulation [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. This means that, in a field-scale model, spatial feedbacks can emerge from the interaction between crop patches, cover crops, field boundaries, and surrounding non-crop vegetation strips, which together influence pest dynamics, pollination, and resource competition [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5]. Therefore, spatial representation matters most when the model is intended to simulate the coexistence of diverse crop species, management zones, and landscape elements, and when the goal is to capture how landscape pattern affects diversification benefits rather than only aggregate yield or soil properties [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

Overall, the model architecture for spatial crop diversification at field scale relies on grid-cell or patch-based discretization, with landscape-level feedbacks captured through land-use change rules and spatial structure [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The strongest implications are that the model must represent patches, heterogeneity, and landscape context, and that spatial resolution and representation matter most when the diversification strategy depends on spatial arrangement rather than uniform management [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5].

Model architecture and functional components supporting diversification

To simulate crop diversification at the field scale, agroecosystem models need compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management, along with mechanisms to represent species interactions, resource competition, and decision rules for crop sequence and spatial allocation. The evidence provided here indicates that agroecosystem models simulate crop growth and development in response to environmental conditions and management practices, including radiation, temperature, water availability, atmospheric CO2, and nutrient availability from soils, and that they incorporate crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other management decisions [N1-F1]. This is directly relevant because diversification requires modeling not only the growth of individual crops but also how they interact with other crops, soil, pests, and management choices.

What model compartments are needed to represent crops, soils, pests, and management? The evidence points to a broad compartmental structure: crop species/cultivars, soil processes, biotic interactions, and management practices. The review explicitly states that agroecosystem models simulate crop growth and development and soil processes in response to environmental conditions and management practices [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that crop diversification is the deliberate introduction of multiple crop species, varieties, and management practices within agricultural systems [N1-R3]. In addition, the same review notes that agroecosystem management can increase beneficial biotic interactions, improve pest management, and decrease reliance on external inputs [N1-R2]. This means that the model must include compartments for crops, soils, pests, and management, and that pest management is especially important for diversification because it can be improved by increasing beneficial biotic interactions [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The evidence also supports the inclusion of cover crops and crop rotations as management strategies, with the review noting that cover crops grown in rotation with cash crops are a realistic strategy to increase agroecosystem diversity [N5-R2]. This implies that management compartments should also include crop rotation, cover crop management, and other diversification practices [N5-R2].

How species interactions and resource competition are modeled? The evidence indicates that agroecosystem models can capture species interactions and competition through biotic interactions, pest dynamics, and resource use efficiency. The review states that spatial and temporal crop diversification can improve resource use efficiency because resources can be allocated according to specific field characteristics [N1-F1]. It also notes that crop diversification improves soil fertility and structure, crop yield, yield stability, nitrogen cycling, carbon sequestration, pest control, biodiversity, and reduced yield risk [N1-F1]. In addition, the review explicitly links crop diversification to improved pest regulation and biodiversity [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that species interactions and resource competition are modeled through pest regulation, competition for nutrients and water, and the broader ecological effects of diversification. The evidence also supports the idea that cover crops can modify the microenvironment and competition among crops [N5-R2], which matters for diversification because it changes the resource landscape and plant-soil feedbacks [N5-R2]. In short, the model must represent how crop species interact with each other and with pests, how they compete for resources, and how management practices alter these interactions [N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-R2].

What management rules or decision rules govern crop sequence and spatial allocation? The evidence shows that management rules and decision rules are central to diversification design. The review states that agroecosystem models are used to understand and design new crop arrangements at field and landscape scale, and that they are useful for quantifying the effects of new crop arrangements on resource use efficiency and ecosystem services [N1-F1]. It also notes that field classification into smaller units based on soil heterogeneities is required for site-specific management [N1-F1]. This implies that the model must include decision rules or management rules that determine how crops are sequenced over time and how they are allocated across space. The evidence also supports crop rotation and cover crop management as decision rules, with crop rotation providing higher diversity over time and cover crops offering potential to improve yield and soil health [N1-R4][N5-R2]. Furthermore, the review mentions that management practices such as crop-cultivar selection, sowing dates, fertilizer applications, irrigation, and other practices are part of agroecosystem models [N1-F1]. These management rules are important because they govern the sequence of crops and the spatial distribution of crop types within a field. The evidence also indicates that the model must account for how management decisions are made in response to soil heterogeneity and field structure [N1-F1].

Taken together, the model architecture needed to support diversification includes crop compartments, soil compartments, pest compartments, and management compartments; it must represent species interactions and resource competition through biotic interactions, pest regulation, and nutrient/water competition; and it must include decision rules or management rules that determine crop sequence and spatial allocation [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R2]. The strongest conclusion is that diversification simulation at the field scale requires a compartmentalized model that integrates crop identity, soil state, pest dynamics, and management decisions, with explicit rules governing how crops are sequenced and where they are placed in the landscape [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R2].
